title: Data Distributions
tagline: The shape of your data – normal, skewed, uniform, bimodal – and why it matters.
what_it_is: A distribution tells you how often each value appears. It's the shape you see when you draw a histogram. Normal looks like a bell. Skewed has a long tail on one side. Uniform is flat. Bimodal has two peaks. The shape decides which summary stats are safe and which models will work.
key_points: Normal (bell) = symmetric, mean = median. Common in nature (heights, errors).
Right skewed = long tail on the right (income). Mean > median.
Left skewed = long tail on the left (test scores where most passed). Mean < median.
Uniform = all values roughly equally common (like dice rolls).
Bimodal = two peaks, often means two different groups mixed together.
Always plot before you assume normality.
why_it_exists: Different distributions break different assumptions. Many statistical tests assume normality. If your data is skewed, using mean as a summary misleads. If it's bimodal, a single average is meaningless. Knowing the shape protects you from stupid mistakes.
visual_alt: Five histograms: normal bell curve (magenta), right skewed with long tail (gold), left skewed with tail to left (purple), uniform flat (green), and bimodal with two peaks (pink).
when_to_use: Before reporting mean vs median – skewed data calls for median.
Before using t‑tests or linear regression (they assume normality).
When you see two peaks – consider splitting your data into two groups.
common_mistakes: Assuming a dataset is normal without checking. Most real data is not.
Using mean on bimodal data – the average of two peaks is a valley nobody lives in.
Ignoring skewness when building linear models – they get pulled toward the tail.
ds_usage: EDA starts with distribution plots. Many ML algorithms perform better with normally distributed features (so people log‑transform skewed data). Clustering algorithms can naturally find the two groups in a bimodal distribution.
